Things we can do: split a string, extract groups, covert to lower case, strip white space. An alternative to splitting might be replacing.

We will want to talk about regular expression as a syntax for matching literal strings or types of characters.

```{python}
phone = pl.DataFrame({
    'name': [' Fay Ken Data', 'Fay k Data ', 'Fay K. Data.', "Fay K D'Ata", ' Fay Data ', 'Fay Kent Data'],
    'ph'  : ['1234567890', '123 456 7890', '123-456-7890', '123.456.7890', '(123)456-7890', '+1 123 4567890']
})
phone
```

Let's try to harmonize these names and numbers so they have a consistent look feel.

Let's start with the name. You can fix the issues in the order the students identify them. I'll deal with the leading and trailing white spaces first.

Point out that the .str. method gives them access to 40+ functions made to deal with string data. Maybe type .str. and talk through many of the functions that are available for autofill.

```{python}
phone_1 = phone.with_columns(pl.col('name').str.strip_chars()
                     # replace the period and apostrophe with empty strings to remove them
                     .str.replace_all(r'\.|\'', "")   #or if you use double quotes you don't need the backslack in front of '. You get a warning if you don't put r in front of the string
                     .str.to_titlecase()
)                     
phone_1
```

Here is a helpful cheatsheet: https://hypebright.nl/en/r-en/ultimate-cheatsheet-for-regex-in-r-2/

Let's split the name into 3 parts

```{python}
phone_2 = phone_1.with_columns(
    pl.col('name').str.extract("([[:alpha:]]+)").alias('first')
    , pl.col('name').str.extract(" ([[:alpha:]]+)$").alias('last')
    , pl.col('name').str.extract("^[[:alpha:]]* ([[:alpha:]]*) [[:alpha:]]*$").alias('middle')
)
phone_2
```

Could I have done this without standardizing the punctuation and capitalization first?? YES
Well, I need to remove the white spaces at the end and beginning or it gets much more difficult

```{python}
phone.with_columns(pl.col('name').str.strip_chars()).with_columns(
    pl.col('name').str.extract("^(\S+)\s").alias('first') #\S is any non-white space character
    , pl.col('name').str.extract("\s(\S*)$").alias('last')
    , pl.col('name').str.extract("^\S* (\S*) \S*$").alias('middle')
)
```

*Optional:
splitn() is a short cut if the names are more consistent. For example, the dataset doesn't include the name with no middle name

```{python}
phone_redux = phone_1.with_row_index().filter(pl.col('index') != 4)

phone_redux.with_columns(
    #pl.col('name').str.split(" ").list.to_struct(upper_bound=3) #split() gives a list
     pl.col('name').str.splitn(" ", 3) #splitn() returns a struct
     .struct.rename_fields(['first', 'middle', 'last'])
).unnest('name')
```

Let's put the phone number into 3 pieces: area code, next 3 digits, and last 4 digits

Probably the simplest thing to do is to remove everything that isn't a number.

```{python}
phone_3 = phone_2.with_columns(
    #pl.col('ph').str.replace_all(" |-|\+|\(|\)|\.", "").alias('nums') #perhaps too hard to read
    pl.col('ph').str.replace_all(r"\D", "") #uses \D to represent any non-digit\
      .str.slice(-10) #gets the last 10 digits
)
phone_3
```

Now all the numbers are in a standard format, I'll try to break them apart into 3 separate pieces:
area code, first 3, and last 4

```{python}
phone_3.with_columns(
    pl.col('ph')
      .str.extract(r"^(\d{3}).*$")     
      .alias('area_code')
    , pl.col('ph')
        .str.extract(r"^\d{3}(\d{3}).*$")
        .alias('next_3')
    , pl.col('ph')
        .str.extract(r"^.*(\d{4})$")
        .alias('last_4')
)
```

But in such a rigid format, here is a much simpler way

```{python}
phone_3.with_columns(
    area_code = pl.col('ph').str.slice(0, 3),
    next_3 = pl.col('ph').str.slice(3,3),
    last_4 = pl.col('ph').str.slice(-4) #negative number reads from the end
)
```
